What it does

Requests the Hawaii Civil Rights Commission to examine whether existing state anti-discrimination laws apply to algorithmic and automated decision systems, and to report findings and recommendations to the Legislature by twenty days before the 2027 Regular Session.

Who it applies to

  • Hawai‘i Civil Rights Commission

Effective date

not stated in the text

Obligations

  • Examine the applicability of existing state anti-discrimination laws to algorithmic and automated decision systems (BE IT RESOLVED clause)
  • Include in the examination an assessment of whether existing state law provides sufficient authority to investigate and remedy discrimination arising from algorithmic or automated determination systems (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 1)
  • Include in the examination identification of potential jurisdictional or evidentiary challenges associated with algorithmic discrimination claims (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 2)
  • Include in the examination evaluation of whether guidance, rulemaking, or administrative clarification may assist individuals and regulated entities in understanding their rights and responsibilities (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 3)
  • Include in the examination consideration of the feasibility of establishing an intake or complaint pathway for alleged algorithmic or automated discrimination under existing state law (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 4)
  • Include in the examination recommendations, if any, for legislative action to ensure civil rights and anti-discrimination protections remain effective (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 5)
  • Submit a report of findings and recommendations, including any proposed legislation, to the Legislature no later than twenty days prior to the convening of the Regular Session of 2027 (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, report deadline)

Penalties and enforcement

Not stated in the text; the resolution does not create penalties, enforcement mechanisms, or a private right of action.

How it affects AI deployment

  • The resolution does not directly impose requirements on organisations deploying AI; it requests a study by the Hawaii Civil Rights Commission that may lead to future guidance, rulemaking, or legislation affecting algorithmic and automated decision systems (BE IT RESOLVED clause and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause)

Compliance steps

  • Conduct an examination of the applicability of existing state anti-discrimination laws to algorithmic and automated decision systems (BE IT RESOLVED clause)
  • Assess whether existing state law provides sufficient authority to investigate and remedy algorithmic discrimination (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 1)
  • Identify potential jurisdictional or evidentiary challenges associated with algorithmic discrimination claims (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 2)
  • Evaluate whether guidance, rulemaking, or administrative clarification may assist individuals and regulated entities (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 3)
  • Consider the feasibility of establishing an intake or complaint pathway for alleged algorithmic or automated discrimination (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 4)
  • Develop recommendations, if any, for legislative action (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, item 5)
  • Submit a report of findings and recommendations, including any proposed legislation, to the Legislature by the deadline (BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED clause, report deadline)

HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES 
 
 
 H.R. NO. 
 
 
 182 
 
 
 
 
 THIRTY-THIRD LEGISLATURE, 2026 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 STATE OF HAWAII 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 

 HOUSE RESOLUTION 

   

   

 requesting the hawai ʻ i civil rights commission to
examine the applicability of existing state anti-discrimination laws to
algorithmic and automated decision systems . 

   

   

   

 

 
 

 

      WHEREAS, Hawaii
has a longstanding commitment to protecting individuals from discrimination in
employment, housing, public accommodations, credit, and access to state and
county services; and 

   

      WHEREAS, the
Hawai ʻ i
Civil Rights Commission is charged with enforcing the State's
anti-discrimination laws and ensuring equal opportunity for all of Hawaii's
residents; and 

   

      WHEREAS, algorithmic
and automated decision systems, including artificial intelligence tools, are
increasingly used in employment screening, tenant selection, credit
determinations, and public benefits eligibility determinations to make
decisions in areas that are traditionally protected by anti-discrimination laws;
and 

   

      WHEREAS, research
and national experience suggests that algorithmic and automated determination
systems may replicate, amplify, or obscure patterns of discrimination,
particularly when these systems are built upon biased data or opaque modeling
practices or lack sufficient oversight; and 

   

      WHEREAS, discrimination
arising from algorithmic and automated decision systems may present novel
jurisdictional, evidentiary, and enforcement questions under the State's
existing civil rights statutes; and 

   

      WHEREAS, ensuring
that civil rights protections remain effective in the face of evolving
technologies is consistent with this body's responsibility to uphold fairness,
equal protection, and public confidence in government; now, therefore, 

   

      BE IT
RESOLVED by the House of Representatives of the Thirty-third Legislature of the
State of Hawaii, Regular Session of 2026, that the Hawai ʻ i Civil Rights
Commission is requested to examine the applicability of existing state
anti-discrimination laws to algorithmic and automated decision systems; and 

   

      BE IT FURTHER
RESOLVED that the examination include, to the extent possible: 

   

      (1)   An assessment of whether existing state law
provides sufficient authority to investigate and remedy discrimination arising
from algorithmic or automated determination systems; 

   

      (2)   Identification of potential jurisdictional or
evidentiary challenges associated with algorithmic discrimination claims; 

   

      (3)   Evaluation of whether guidance, rulemaking, or
administrative clarification may assist individuals and regulated entities in
understanding their rights and responsibilities; 

   

      (4)   Consideration of the feasibility of
establishing an intake or complaint pathway for alleged algorithmic or
automated discrimination under existing state law; and 

   

      (5)   Recommendations, if any, for legislative
action to ensure civil rights and anti-discrimination protections remain
effective; and 

   

      BE IT FURTHER
RESOLVED that the Hawai ʻ i
Civil Rights Commission is requested to submit a report of its findings and
recommendations, including any proposed legislation, to the Legislature no
later than twenty days prior to the convening of the Regular Session of 2027;
and 

   

      BE IT FURTHER
RESOLVED that certified copies of this Resolution be transmitted to the Chair
of the Hawai ʻ i
Civil Rights Commission and Executive Director of the Hawai ʻ i
Civil Rights Commission. 

   

   

   

 
 
 
   
 
 
 OFFERED BY: 
 
 
 _____________________________
